read.sections.0.text.source:
A history painting presents an account of the past through figures, setting and arrangement. Its artist chooses which moment to show and whose actions seem important. Two paintings of Prince Diponegoro's capture show how such choices can support power. They can also challenge its public image. The pictures also have histories of their own. Later audiences can give them meanings that their first viewers would not have shared.

Diponegoro was a Javanese prince and a major leader of resistance during the Java War of 1825–1830. Dutch colonial authorities sought to control Java, where local rulers and communities had their own interests. Colonial rule means control of a territory by an outside power. On 28 March 1830, Diponegoro was arrested at Magelang during talks. He had been given a promise of safe conduct: a promise that he could come and go safely. The arrest helped bring the war to an end. It happened in the Dutch East Indies, long before Indonesia proclaimed its independence in 1945.
read.sections.0.text.note: Magelang = เมืองมาเกอลัง (no established Thai name; check). Dutch East Indies = หมู่เกาะอินเดียตะวันออกของดัตช์. safe conduct = สัญญาว่าจะเดินทางได้อย่างปลอดภัย. glossary colonial rule = การปกครองแบบอาณานิคม (KEY_TERMS).
read.sections.0.text.back:
History paintings present a story about the past through the figures in the picture, the setting and the arrangement. The artist chooses which moment to show and whose actions look important. Two paintings of the arrest of Prince Diponegoro show that choices like these can support power, and can also challenge the public image of power. The pictures themselves have their own history too. Later viewers may give a picture meanings the first viewers did not think of in the same way.

Prince Diponegoro was a Javanese prince and an important leader of the resistance in the Java War. Between 1825 and 1830, Dutch colonial officials tried to control Java, where rulers and local communities had their own interests. Colonial rule means power from outside coming in to control a land. On 28 March 1830 Prince Diponegoro was arrested in the town of Magelang during negotiations, even though he had been promised safe travel, that is, a promise that he could come and go back safely. This arrest helped end the war. The event happened in the Dutch East Indies, long before Indonesia declared independence in 1945.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A history painting tells a story about the past. The artist picks one moment and who looks important. Two paintings show the capture of Prince Diponegoro. Art can back up power or question it. Later, people gave the paintings new meanings.

Diponegoro was a prince from Java. He led a fight against Dutch control in the Java War, from 1825 to 1830. Colonial rule means rule of a land by an outside power. Dutch officials wanted to rule Java. But the rulers and people of Java had their own goals. On 28 March 1830, Diponegoro came to Magelang for talks. The Dutch had promised he would be safe. But they arrested him. This helped end the war. Then, the land was called the Dutch East Indies. Indonesia became free much later, in 1945.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
History paintings tell stories about the past. The artist chooses one moment and chooses who looks important. Two paintings show the arrest of Prince Diponegoro. Art can support power or question power. Later, people gave these paintings new meanings.

Prince Diponegoro came from Java. In the Java War, between 1825 and 1830, the prince led the fight against Dutch control. Colonial rule is when power from outside governs a land. Dutch officials wanted to govern Java, but the rulers and people of Java had their own goals. On 28 March 1830 the prince came to the town of Magelang to negotiate. The Dutch side promised the prince would be safe, but they arrested him. This helped end the war. At that time this land was called the Dutch East Indies. Indonesia gained independence a long time after that, in 1945.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Two artists, two kinds of commission

read.sections.1.text.source:
The Dutch artist Nicolaas Pieneman painted his version around 1830–1835. It was a commission for General Hendrik Merkus de Kock. He was the officer who ordered the arrest. Its familiar title, The Submission of Prince Dipo Negoro to General De Kock, encourages viewers to see the scene as a surrender. Upright Dutch officers, the raised Dutch flag and followers gathered below make colonial authority look certain. The commission matters: this was an account made for the victorious commander.

Raden Saleh completed The Arrest of Prince Diponegoro in 1857. Saleh came from Java. He built his painting career through training and patronage in Europe. He worked across connected but unequal worlds. Both praise in Europe and his ties to his homeland shaped his career. His life does not fit a simple split between a European way of painting and a separate Javanese view. Oil painting could carry an account that questioned colonial power.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The Dutch artist Nicolaas Pieneman painted his picture in about 1830–1835. This picture was a commission from General Hendrik Merkus de Kock, the officer who ordered the arrest. The familiar title, The Submission of Prince Dipo Negoro to General De Kock, invites viewers to see this scene as a surrender. The Dutch officers standing upright, the Dutch flag raised high and the followers gathered below make colonial power look secure and certain. So the commission matters, because this is a story made for the commander of the winning side.

Raden Saleh finished painting The Arrest of Prince Diponegoro in 1857. This artist came from Java. He built his career as a painter through training and patronage in Europe. He worked between worlds that were connected but unequal. Both praise in Europe and his ties to his homeland shaped his career. His life does not fit a simple division between a European way of painting and a separate Javanese view. An oil painting could tell a story that questioned colonial power.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
A Dutch artist, Nicolaas Pieneman, painted his version in about 1830 to 1835. It was a commission from General De Kock. He ordered the arrest. A commission is a request to make a work. The title calls the scene a submission. That means giving up. Dutch officers stand tall. A Dutch flag flies high. His followers are lower down. So Dutch power looks sure and strong. The painting was made for the winner.

Raden Saleh finished his painting in 1857. Saleh came from Java. He trained in Europe, and people there paid for his art. He lived between two worlds that were not equal. He won praise in Europe, but he felt close to his home. So we cannot just call his art Dutch or Javanese. His oil painting could question Dutch power.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Between 1830 and 1835, a Dutch artist named Nicolaas Pieneman painted his picture. This picture was a commission from General De Kock, who ordered the prince's arrest. A commission is a request to make a work. The title calls this scene a submission. This word means giving up. Dutch officers stand upright. The Dutch flag waves high. The prince's followers are lower down. So Dutch power looks secure and strong. This picture was made for the winning side.

In 1857 Raden Saleh finished his picture. This artist came from Java. He trained in painting in Europe, and people there paid to buy his work. He lived between two unequal worlds. He was praised in Europe but also felt tied to his homeland. So we cannot simply call his work Dutch-style or Javanese-style. His oil painting could question Dutch power.

read.sections.2.text.source:
In Saleh's composition, Diponegoro stands upright near De Kock, surrounded by distressed followers. His white clothing and firm posture give him dignity at the moment of capture. The crowd brings the emotional cost of the arrest into the foreground. Unlike Pieneman, Saleh includes no flying Dutch flag. These differences help explain why scholars see the later painting as a challenge to the earlier one. That reading connects visible choices with historical context. A painted face alone cannot prove what a person actually felt.

The painting's later life matters too. The Dutch government returned Saleh's work to Indonesia in 1978. Diponegoro's image has appeared on posters, monuments and other artworks. It has helped later generations debate heroism, resistance and national identity. National identity means the ideas and memories through which people feel they belong to a nation. Such uses belong to Indonesia's changing history. They do not prove that Saleh held every later nationalist belief. Neither painting speaks for every Dutch or Javanese person. Neither gives a complete, neutral history of the war. Together, they show how art takes part in struggles over whose account becomes public memory.
read.sections.2.text.note: glossary national identity = อัตลักษณ์ของชาติ (KEY_TERMS). nationalist = ชาตินิยม; heroism = ความเป็นวีรบุรุษ. In the simpler text "the fight for freedom" = การต่อสู้เพื่อเอกราช.
read.sections.2.text.back:
In Saleh's composition, Prince Diponegoro stands upright near De Kock, surrounded by distressed followers. The white clothes and firm stance make the prince look dignified at the moment of arrest. The crowd brings the emotional pain of the arrest into the front of the picture. Saleh's picture has no Dutch flag flying like Pieneman's. These differences help explain why scholars see the later picture as a challenge to the earlier one. That interpretation connects what the artist chose to show with the historical context. A painted face alone cannot prove how that person really felt.

The picture's later life matters too. The Netherlands government returned Saleh's work to Indonesia in 1978. Images of Prince Diponegoro appeared on posters, monuments and other artworks. This picture helped later generations debate heroism, resistance and national identity. National identity means the ideas and memories that make people feel they are part of a nation. Using the picture this way is part of Indonesia's changing history, but it does not prove Saleh held all the nationalist beliefs that came later. No picture speaks for all Dutch or all Javanese people, and no picture gives a complete, neutral history of the war. Seen together, the two pictures show that art took part in the struggle over whose story would become society's memory.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Saleh's composition is different. A composition is how the parts of a picture are arranged. The prince stands tall near De Kock. He wears white. The men and women around him are upset. This gives him dignity, even as he is caught. The crowd shows how painful the arrest was. Saleh's painting has no Dutch flag. So experts say it pushes back against Pieneman's story. But a painted face cannot prove what a real person felt.

Later, in 1978, the Dutch government gave it back to Indonesia. The prince's picture has been on posters and statues. People use it to talk about heroes and the fight for freedom. They also talk about national identity. That means the ideas that make people feel part of a nation. This does not prove what Saleh believed. Neither painting speaks for all Dutch or all Javanese people. Neither tells the whole story of the war. People still argue about whose story is remembered.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Saleh's composition is different. Composition is the arrangement of the parts of a picture. The prince stands upright near De Kock. The prince wears white clothes. The men and women around the prince look sad. This makes the prince look dignified even when being arrested. The crowd shows how painful the arrest was. Saleh's picture has no Dutch flag. So experts say this picture argues against the story Pieneman told. But faces in a painting cannot prove how the real people felt.

Later, in 1978, the Netherlands government returned this picture to Indonesia. Pictures of the prince were on posters and statues. People used this picture to talk about heroes and the fight for independence. They also talked about national identity. National identity is the ideas that make people feel part of a nation. This does not prove what the artist believed. No picture speaks for all Dutch people or all Javanese people. No picture can tell the whole story of the war. People still argue about whose story will be remembered.

write.prompt.source: In two or three sentences, explain how one difference between these paintings changes the story of the arrest. Say who a painting was made by or for.
write.prompt.back: Write two or three sentences explaining how one difference between these two paintings changes the story of the arrest. Also say who painted the picture, or whom the picture was painted for.

write.example.source: In Pieneman's painting, Dutch officers stand tall under a Dutch flag. The prince's followers are lower down. Pieneman painted it for General De Kock, who ordered the arrest. So the scene looks like a surrender. In Saleh's painting, there is no Dutch flag, and the prince stands tall in white. This matters because it gives him dignity. It also shows the arrest as a painful moment for his followers.
write.example.back: In Pieneman's painting, Dutch officers stand upright under the Dutch flag. The prince's followers are lower down. Pieneman painted this picture for General De Kock, who ordered the arrest. So the scene looks like a surrender. In Saleh's painting there is no Dutch flag, and the prince stands upright in white clothes. This matters because it makes the prince look dignified. The picture also shows that the arrest was a painful moment for the prince's followers.

visual.alt.source: Oil painting. Prince Diponegoro, in white, stands at the top of the steps of a veranda on the same level as Dutch officers, one of whom gestures toward a waiting carriage. His followers crowd the steps and ground below, some kneeling and one woman clinging to him, with mountains in the distance.
visual.alt.back: An oil painting. Prince Diponegoro in white clothes stands on the top step of a veranda, at the same level as the Dutch officers. One officer gestures toward a waiting carriage. The prince's followers crowd on the steps and the ground below; some kneel, and a woman clings to the prince. Mountains in the distance.

Prince Diponegoro, in white clothes and a green turban, stands lower down among followers, some kneeling. Spears lie on the ground and soldiers stand in a row on the left.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Colonial conquest and war: teach colonial rule as an unequal relationship of power. Keep the arrest and the war non-graphic, with no reenactment or role-play. Keep the documented breach of safe conduct (Diponegoro was arrested during negotiations despite a promise of safe conduct) apart from interpretations of poses and faces. Don't describe the Java War as a conflict between two modern nation-states: in 1830 Java was part of the Dutch East Indies, and Indonesia proclaimed independence in 1945.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Colonial conquest and war: teach colonial rule as an unequal power relationship. Tell the story of the arrest and the war without violent detail; no re-enactment or role-play. Separate the documented broken promise of safety (Diponegoro was arrested during negotiations although he had been promised safe travel) from interpretation of gestures and faces. Do not describe the Java War as a conflict between two modern nation-states, because in 1830 Java was part of the Dutch East Indies, and Indonesia declared independence in 1945.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Identity and belief: Diponegoro was also an Islamic religious leader. No learner is asked to speak for his faith or community, to share their own religion, identity or family, or to represent Indonesians, Javanese or Dutch people. For many learners in Indonesia, Diponegoro is a national hero; treat that later memory as real history to learn about, while keeping it apart from what the 1830 sources show. Accept reasoned answers about either painting without requiring a feeling about it.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Identity and belief: Diponegoro was also an Islamic religious leader. Do not ask any learner to speak for his religion or community, to tell about their own religion, identity or family, or to represent Indonesians, Javanese or Dutch people. For many learners in Indonesia Diponegoro is a national hero. Treat this later memory as real history worth learning, but keep it apart from what the 1830 evidence shows. Accept reasoned answers about either picture without requiring learners to feel a particular way about a picture.

educatorNotes.0.source: Don't use Saleh's European training to dismiss his viewpoint, or assume that his Javanese origins make every detail of his painting factual. Later nationalist readings of the painting and Saleh's own intentions are separate questions; the reading keeps them apart.
educatorNotes.0.back: Do not use Saleh's training in Europe as a reason to dismiss his point of view, and do not assume that his coming from Java makes every detail in the picture a fact. Later nationalist interpretations of the picture and Saleh's own intentions are different questions; the reading keeps the two apart.

Require a reasoned connection, not a set feeling about either painting.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: accept explanations supported by evidence about stance, grouping, the flag, the followers or the emphasis on emotion; connecting De Kock's commission with Pieneman's surrender-like picture, or connecting Saleh's choices with Diponegoro's dignity and the pain of the arrest. A reasoned connection is wanted, not a set feeling about either picture.

educatorNotes.2.source: Sources: the Rijksmuseum record gives Pieneman's commission, the safe conduct, the current title and the date range c. 1830–c. 1835 (some older records say 1835). Elly Kent's article (National Gallery Singapore) supports the missing flag, the scholars' reading and the later uses. The Cabinet Secretariat page supports the capture place and date, the 1857 date and the 1978 return; the lesson does not adopt its claims that particular colours prove one intention, or its incorrect claim that Islam forbids all fighting during Ramadan, and its photographs are not used. The 1945 proclamation is from the State Secretariat (setneg.go.id).
educatorNotes.2.back: Sources: the Rijksmuseum record gives Pieneman's commission, the safe-conduct promise, the current title and the date range c. 1830 to c. 1835 (some older records say 1835). Elly Kent's essay (National Gallery Singapore) supports the absent flag, scholars' interpretation and the picture's later use. The Cabinet Secretariat web page supports the place and date of the arrest, 1857 and the 1978 return. The lesson does not take up that page's claim that certain colours prove a particular intention, or its incorrect claim that Islam forbids all fighting in Ramadan, and does not use photos from that page. The 1945 independence information comes from the State Secretariat (setneg.go.id).

educatorNotes.3.source: Images: both are Wikimedia Commons' faithful reproductions of two-dimensional public-domain paintings (Saleh died in 1880, Pieneman in 1860), so the credit links the exact Commons file pages, where the rights statements are. Indonesian sources place Saleh's painting at the Yogyakarta Presidential Palace and at Istana Negara, Jakarta: one work, so the caption gives no fixed display place. Commons reports a heritage registration, RNCB.20190219.01.001562, which is not a museum accession number. Don't swap in the separate "Rijksmuseum Official" Commons file of Pieneman's painting, which carries a CC BY 3.0 statement.
educatorNotes.3.back: Images: both are faithful reproductions on Wikimedia Commons of two-dimensional paintings in the public domain (Saleh died in 1880 and Pieneman in 1860), so the credits link to the matching Commons file pages, which carry the rights statements. Indonesian sources place Saleh's picture both at the Presidential Palace in Yogyakarta and at the Istana Negara in Jakarta; it is the same work, so the caption does not give an exact display location. Commons reports heritage registration number RNCB.20190219.01.001562, which is not a museum object number.
